rationale: The paper centrally analyzes cost-reflective pricing, household water metering, tariff differentiation, and inter-regional/inter-household cross-subsidisation in England and Wales (fees_tariffs_subsidies), while situating these pricing reforms within post-1989 privatisation and market environmentalism (regulatory_model_ownership) and examining statutory hosepipe bans during the 2006 drought alongside the UK ban on domestic disconnections (enforcement_sanctions). The focal access outcome is household economic_access—specifically regional disparities in water and sewerage bills and the rising share of low-income households spending over 3% of disposable income on water—evaluated alongside household water demand practices. Empirically, the study employs mixed_methods, combining quantitative secondary statistics from OFWAT/Defra/Environment Agency and a 100-home micro-component water-metering database with qualitative interviews of 22 households and 4 water-company resource teams during the 2006 southeast England drought.
